Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 1:

(p-325) Surat Maryam

Surat Maryam, upon her be peace, is Meccan, and it has either ninety-eight or ninety-nine verses. [According to] Madani and Shami [readings/counts], it is [the same].

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ayn, Sad.﴾ Al-Suddi said: it is the Greatest Name of Allah. It was also said: it is the name of the surah. 'Ali and Yahya read the ha' and the ya' with a kasra; Nafi' read between the fatha and the kasra, closer to the fatha; Abu 'Amr read the ha' with a kasra and the ya' with a fatha; Hamza did the reverse of this; and the others read both with a fatha.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 2:

﴿This is a mention of the mercy of your Lord﴾ is the predicate of an implied subject, meaning: this is a mention. ﴿to His servant﴾ is the object of the noun "mercy" (raḥmah). ﴿Zakariyya﴾ — with the short vowel (read as Zakariyya without the long alif, i.e., qaṣr) is recited by Ḥamzah, ʿAlī and Ḥafṣ, and it is in apposition (badal) to "His servant."

﴿When﴾ is a temporal adverb (ẓarf) governed by "mercy." ﴿He called upon his Lord with a secret call﴾: he supplicated Him in a private whisper, as he had been commanded, and this is further from ostentation (riya') and closer to sincerity of heart (safa'). Or he concealed it so that he would not be blamed for asking for a child in his old age, for he was seventy-five or eighty years old.

﴿He said, "My Lord"﴾ This explains the supplication. Its underlying form is يا رَبِّي (yā rabbī, "O my Lord"), so the vocative particle and the possessive pronoun were omitted for brevity.

﴿Indeed my bones have weakened within me﴾: ضَعُفَ (weakened). The bones are singled out because they are the pillar of the body, on which its stability rests. When they weaken, it collapses and its strength falls away. Also, the bone is the hardest and firmest part of the body, so if it has weakened, what lies beyond it is weaker still. He used the singular, عَظْم (ʿaẓm, "bone"), because the singular indicates the genus, meaning that this kind of bone, which is the pillar and the support, and from which the body is most firmly constructed, has been afflicted by weakness.

﴿And the head has blazed with grey hair﴾: شَيْبًا (shayban) is a tamyīz (a specifying accusative clarifying the noun it follows). The meaning is that grey hair has spread across my head. The verb اشْتَعَلَتِ (ishtaʿalat) is used of fire when it scatters while burning and becomes separate flames. The grey hair is likened to the flames of fire in its whiteness, in its spreading through the hair, and in its taking every direction through the hair, just as fire spreads. You will not find a more eloquent expression than this. Consider that the original sentence would be: "O Lord, I have grown old," since old age involves the weakness of the body and the greying of the head that accompanies it. A more emphatic form would be: "My body has weakened and my head has turned grey." A stronger one still would be: "My bones of body have weakened," which contains a shift away from direct statement to kināya (metonymy), and is therefore more forceful. Stronger still: "I, the bones of my body have weakened." Stronger: "Indeed the bones of my body have weakened," which combines the general and the particular. Stronger: "Indeed the bones have weakened from my body," which omits the intermediary "body." Stronger still: "Indeed the bone has weakened within me," because weakness encompasses the bones individually, one by one. By treating the plural as singular, the statement is grounded in the fact that weakness of the whole can be realised through a part, not every single bone. For this reason, the literal form in "my head has turned grey" (shāba raʾsī) was abandoned in favour of the more eloquent form, which is isti'āra (metaphor). The result is: "the greying of my head has blazed." An even more eloquent form is: "my head has blazed with grey hair," in which the blazing is attributed to the place where the hair grows and springs forth, which is the head, to convey that the blazing encompasses the whole head. The parallel is: "the greying of my head has blazed" and "my head has blazed with grey," just as "the fire has blazed in my house" and "my house has blazed with fire." The distinction is clear. It also contains both the general and the particular, as is known in the discussion of tamyīz. An even more eloquent form is: "and the head has blazed with grey hair from me," for the reason already mentioned. Yet more eloquent is: "and the head has blazed with grey hair," where the addressee is left to know that this is the head of Zakariyyā, by the context of its being conjoined to "the weakening of the bone."

﴿And I have never been, in my supplication to You, my Lord, unfortunate﴾: دُعائِكَ (duʿāʾika) is a verbal noun, and its genitive form is an annexation to the object, meaning "in my supplicating You." ﴿shaqiyyan﴾: that is, I have always been one whose supplication was answered before this day, happy in it and not unfortunate. It is said: saʿida fulān bi-ḥājatihi (so-and-so was made happy by his need) when he attained it, and shaqiya (was unfortunate) when he failed and did not obtain it. It is related from some scholars that a needy man asked someone and said: "I am the one whom you treated well at such-and-such a time." He said: "Welcome to one who sought a means through us to us at the time of his need," and fulfilled his need.

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿And indeed I fear my relatives (al-mawali) after me﴾. They are his ʿasabah (paternal kinsmen): his brothers and the sons of his paternal uncle. They were among the worst of the Children of Israel, so he feared that they would alter the religion and would not govern his community well. Therefore he asked for a righteous offspring from his own loins, who would be followed in reviving the religion. ﴿From behind me﴾ means after my death. It is read with the qasr (shortened form) and with fath on the ya', as in "hudaya," by Ibn Kathir (Meccan reader). This adverbial phrase does not relate to "khiftu" (I feared), because the existence of his fear after his death is inconceivable. Rather, it relates either to something omitted, or to the meaning of guardianship in "al-mawali," i.e., "I feared the conduct of the mawali, which is their alteration and bad governance, after me," or "I feared those who will be in charge of the matter after me."

﴿And my wife is barren﴾: she is ʿaqir (sterile), unable to bear children. ﴿So grant me from Yourself﴾: by an invention from You without a cause, because my wife is not fit for childbearing. ﴿An heir (waliyyan)﴾: a son who will take charge of your affairs after me.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 6:

﴿Who shall inherit from me and inherit from the family of Ya'qub (Jacob)﴾ With both verbs in the indicative (raf') they are a description (sifah) of waliyyan (an heir): that is, "Grant me a son who will inherit from me the knowledge, and from the family of Ya'qub the prophethood." The meaning of inheriting prophethood is that he is fit to have revelation sent to him; it does not mean that prophethood itself is inherited. With both verbs in the jussive (jazm), Abu 'Amr and 'Ali read them, taking them as an answer (jawab) to the supplication. It is said: "waritu-hu" and "warithtu minhu" (I inherited from him).

﴿from the family of Ya'qub﴾: Ya'qub ibn Ishaq (Jacob, son of Isaac).

﴿And make him, my Lord, one with whom You are pleased﴾: marḍiyyan (one who is accepted), whom You approve of, or radiyan (one who is content) with You and with Your decree.

Then God answered his supplication and said, ﴿O Zakariyya, indeed We give you good tidings of a boy whose name is Yahya﴾. He Himself undertook to name him, as an honour to him. Hamza read "nubashshiruka" with the lightened (single-consonant) form.

﴿We have not made for him before [this] any namesake﴾. No one had been named Yahya before him. This is evidence that a rare name deserves to be preferred (for the one who bears it). It has also been said that "samiyyan" means "equal" or "like": he had no equal in that he never disobeyed, never intended to commit a sin at all, that he was born to an elderly man and an old woman, and that he was chaste (ḥaṣūr). Then, when the angels gave him this good tidings...

Zakariyya said: "My Lord, how can I have a son, when my wife is barren and I have reached extreme old age?"

﴿قالَ رَبِّ أنّى﴾ "how" here means "in what way" (كَيْفَ) ﴿يَكُونُ لِي غُلامٌ﴾ "can I have a boy?" This is not an expression of disbelief (istib'ad) but of inquiry (istikshaf): he was asking in what manner a son would be granted to him, whether while he and his wife remained in their present state, or whether they would be transformed back into young people.

﴿وَكانَتِ امْرَأتِي عاقِرًا وقَدْ بَلَغْتُ مِنَ الكِبَرِ عِتِيًّا﴾ "My wife has been barren, and I have reached old age of extreme decrepitude." That is, I have reached ʿitiyy (عِتِيًّا), which is dryness and stiffness in the joints and bones, like a dry stick, due to old age and advanced years.

The words "ʿitiyyan" (عِتِيًّا), "ṣiliyyan" (صِلِيًّا), "jithiyyan" (جِثِيًّا) and "bukiyyan" (بُكِيًّا) are read with a kasra on the first letter by Ḥamzah, ʿAlī and Ḥafṣ, except in "bukiyyan" (بُكِيًّا).

Qur'anic quotations with ﴿ ﴾ markers: keep markers and translate meaning.

Translation:

﴿He said: "Thus"﴾ The kaf is in the nominative (raf'), meaning: the matter is thus, confirming him (Zakariyya's report). Then he begins: ﴿"Your Lord said"﴾. Or it is in the accusative (nasb) governed by "qala" (said), and "dhalika" (thus) is a reference to something vague (mubham) which it explains: ﴿"It is easy for Me"﴾, meaning: creating Yahya from two aged parents is easy. ﴿"And I created you before, when you were nothing"﴾, meaning: I brought you into existence before (the birth of) Yahya. "We created you" (khalaqnaka) is the reading of Hamzah and Ali. ﴿"And you were nothing"﴾, because that which does not exist is not a thing.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 10:

﴿He said: "My Lord, appoint for me a sign."﴾ A sign (ʿalāma) by which I may know of my wife's pregnancy. ﴿He said: "Your sign is that you shall not speak to people for three nights, while sound (sawiyyan)."﴾ "Sound" is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the pronoun in "tukallima" (speak), meaning: while you are sound in your limbs and tongue. That is, your sign is that you will be prevented from speech, so that you are unable to speak while your bodily members are whole, with no muteness (kharas) or dumbness (bakam) affecting you. The mention of "nights" here, and of "days" in Surat Al ʿImran, indicates that the prohibition from speech lasted three days and their nights, since mentioning the days includes the nights corresponding to them, and likewise mentioning the nights includes the days corresponding to them, by customary usage (ʿurf).

Then he came out to his people from the prayer niche (al-mihrab), from the place of his prayer, and they had been waiting for him, and he was not able to speak. ﴿So he signaled to them﴾: he indicated with his finger. ﴿That glorify [Allah]﴾: pray. The "an" (that) here is the explanatory one (al-mufassira). ﴿Morning and evening﴾: the dawn prayer and the afternoon prayer.

Yā Yaḥyā: meaning, We bestowed upon him Yaḥyā, and We said to him after his birth, at the time of address, ﴿O Yahya﴾, ﴿take the Book﴾, the Tawrah (Torah), ﴿with strength﴾. Here *bi-quwwah* is a *ḥāl* (circumstantial qualifier), meaning: with diligence and firm retention, through success and support. ﴿And We gave him the judgment﴾, meaning wisdom, which is the understanding of the Tawrah and the knowledge of religion. ﴿As a child﴾, *ṣabiyyan*, is also a *ḥāl*. It is said that the children called him to play while he was still a child, and he said, "We were not created for play." (p-٣٢٩)

ww﻿"And tenderness" — compassion and mercy toward his parents and others. It is coordinated with "the judgment" (al-Hukm). ﴿From Us﴾ — from Our presence. ﴿And purity﴾ — purity and righteousness, so that he did not commit any sin. ﴿And he was pious﴾ — submissive and obedient to God.
﴿And dutiful to his parents﴾, and dutiful to them, not disobeying them. ﴿He was not arrogant﴾, proud, ﴿disobedient﴾, disobedient to his Lord.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 15:

﴿And peace be upon him﴾: a security from Allah for him ﴿on the day he was born﴾ from Satan touching him; ﴿and the day he dies﴾ from the two questioners of the grave (fattanay al-qabr); ﴿and the day he is raised up alive﴾ from the greatest terror (al-fazaʿ al-akbar). Ibn ʿUyaynah said: indeed, these are the most frightening of stations.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 16:

﴿And mention﴾ O Muhammad, ﴿in the Book﴾ (the Qur'an) ﴿Maryam﴾ (Mary). That is, recite to them in the Qur'an the story of Maryam, so that they may come to know it and learn what befell her. ﴿When﴾ (idh) is a substitute (badal) for Maryam, a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal), since times include what occurs within them. And in this there is the implication that the purpose of mentioning Maryam is mentioning her time, because this wondrous story occurred during it. ﴿She withdrew from her family﴾ (intabadhat min ahliha), that is, she isolated herself ﴿to a place﴾ (makanan), which is an adverbial accusative (zarf), ﴿eastward﴾ (sharqiyyan), that is, she secluded herself for worship in a place to the east of Bayt al-Maqdis, or from within her house, withdrawn from people. It was also said that she sat in its eastern part to perform the ritual bath from menstruation.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 17:

﴿So she took a screen apart from them﴾ She placed between herself and her family a screen that would conceal her, so that she could bathe behind it. ﴿Then We sent to her Our Spirit﴾ Jibril (peace be upon him). The attribution (idafah) is for honour. He was called "spirit" because religion is given life by him and by his revelation. ﴿So he appeared before her as a perfect man﴾ That is: Jibril took on for her the form of a human being, a beardless young man of handsome face and curly hair. ﴿Sawiyyan﴾ with well-proportioned creation. He was given the form of a human so that she would be at ease with his speech and not shrink from him. Had he appeared to her in the form of the angels, she would have fled from him and would not have been able to bear listening to his speech. (p-330)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 18:

﴿She said: "Indeed, I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, if you are God-fearing."﴾ That is: if there is hope from you that you will fear God, then I seek refuge in Him from you.

"Said" [Jibril, peace be upon him]: "I am only the messenger of your Lord," [meaning he reassured her from what she feared, and informed her that he is not a human being but a messenger from the One whom she sought refuge in]. "That I may give you" [a pure son], by the permission of Allah the Exalted; or [it means] "so that I may be a cause for the giving of a boy through the blowing into the shirt (dir')." [Reading] "li-yahaba laki" (so that He may give you), i.e., Allah: Abu 'Amr and Nafi' [read it this way]. "A pure boy" [i.e., pure from sins], or "one growing upon goodness and blessing."

﴿She said: "How"﴾ meaning: how ﴿can I have a boy﴾, a son, ﴿when no man has touched me﴾, meaning no husband through marriage, ﴿and I have not been unchaste﴾, meaning a woman who commits fornication and seeks men, i.e. seeks sexual gratification from any man. A child does not ordinarily come about except from one of these two. The word *baghiyy* (unchaste woman) is on the pattern *fa'ul*. According to al-Mubarrad, its original form was *baghuwy*, which was changed by transposition (*qalb*) and assimilation (*idgham*), and the *ghayn* was given a kasra (*kasrah*) to match the following vowel (*itba'*). For this reason the feminine *ta'* (*ta' al-ta'nith*) is not attached to it, just as it is not attached in *imra'ah sabur* and *shakur* (a patient woman and a grateful woman). According to others, it is on the pattern *fa'il*, and the *ha'* (*ha' al-ta'nith*) is not attached to it because it has the meaning of *maf'ulah* (passive). Even if it has the meaning of *fa'ilah* (active), it may be treated as analogous to that, as in the verse ﴿Indeed, the mercy of God is near﴾ [al-A'raf: 56].

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 21:

﴿Said﴾ [Jibril], ﴿"Thus it is"﴾, i.e., the matter is as you said: no man has touched you, neither in lawful marriage (nikah) nor in unlawful intercourse (sifah). ﴿Your Lord says: "It is easy for Me"﴾, i.e., granting a child without a father is easy for Me. ﴿And so that We may make him a sign for the people﴾: this is a statement of purpose (ta'lil) whose object (mu'allal) is omitted, i.e., "And so that We may make him a sign for the people, We did that." Or it is conjoined with a implied purpose, i.e., "So that We may show by it Our power, and so that We may make him a sign for the people," meaning a lesson (ibrah) and a proof (burhan) of Our power. ﴿And a mercy from Us﴾ for whoever believes in him. ﴿And it was﴾ the creation of Isa ﴿a matter decreed﴾, determined and inscribed in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh).

(p-331) Then, when she was reassured by his words, he blew into the opening of her garment, and the breath reached her womb.

﴿So she conceived him﴾, that is, the one granted (al-mawhub), and her age was thirteen years, or ten, or twenty. ﴿And she withdrew with him﴾, that is, she secluded herself while he was in her womb. The prepositional phrase (al-jarr wa'l-majrur, "with him") is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: the duration of the pregnancy was one hour; as she conceived him, she cast him off. It was also said six months, and it was said seven, and it was said eight. No child born at eight months lived except 'Isa. It was also said she conceived him in one hour and gave birth to him in one hour. ﴿To a remote place﴾, far from her family, behind the mountain. This was because, when she sensed the pregnancy, she fled from her people for fear of blame.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 23:

﴿So she brought her to﴾ (fa-ajā'ahā): he brought her [to it]. It is also said that it means "compelled her" (alja'ahā). It is a verb derived from jā'a (to come), but after being transferred (naql) to the sense of compulsion (al-ilja'), its usage changed. Do you not see that you do not say "jiotu al-makān" (I came to the place) and "ajā'anīhi Zayd" (Zayd brought me to it)?

﴿the pains of childbirth﴾ (al-makhād): the pain of labour.

﴿to the trunk of the palm tree﴾ (ila jidh'i al-nakhla): its root/trunk. It was dry, and the time was winter. The definite form indicates that it was a well-known palm tree. It is also permissible that the definite article is generic (li-l-jins), meaning: the trunk of this kind of tree, as if the Exalted had guided her to the palm tree so that she might feed herself its fresh dates, for they are the food of the woman in childbirth (khursat al-nufasā', i.e., her food).

Then ﴿she said﴾, in anguish at what had befallen her: ﴿Would that I had died before this﴾ (yawm) [this day]. Madani and Kufi readers, except Abu Bakr, read it with a kasra on the mim (mitt); the others read it with a damma (muttu). It is said: māta yamūtu and māta yamātu.

﴿and I had been a thing forgotten, utterly forgotten﴾ (nasyan mansiyyan): a thing abandoned, not known and not mentioned. With a fatha on the nun (nasyan): Hamza and Hafs; with a kasra: the others. Their meaning is one and the same: a thing that is due to be cast aside and forgotten because of its insignificance.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 24:**

﴿Then he called to her from beneath her﴾, that is, the one beneath her. The word "man" (من) is the subject (fa'il, the grammatical subject), and it refers to Jibril, peace be upon him, because he was in a place lower than her, or to Isa, peace be upon him, because he addressed her from beneath her garment (dhayl). "Min tahtiha" (مِن تَحْتِها) is read by Madani and Kufi readers except Abu Bakr, and the subject is then a concealed pronoun (mudmar), which is Isa, peace be upon him, or Jibril. The pronoun in "tahtiha" (تَحْتِها) refers to the palm tree. Because of the severity of what she had suffered, she was comforted by His saying ﴿Do not grieve﴾, meaning do not be concerned about the solitude, the lack of food and drink, and the talk of the people. The "an" (أنْ) here has the meaning of "i.e." (أيْ).

﴿Your Lord has placed beneath you﴾, meaning, close to you, or under your command: if you order it to flow, it flows, and if you order it to stand still, it stands still. ﴿a stream (sariyyan)﴾, meaning a small river according to the majority (al-Jumhur). The Prophet ﷺ was asked about the sari, and he said: "It is the jadwal (a small stream)." It is also reported from al-Hasan that it means a noble master, referring to Isa, peace be upon him. It is narrated that Khalid ibn Safwan said to him: "The Arabs call the jadwal sari," and al-Hasan said: "You are right," and returned to his (earlier) opinion. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: Isa or Jibril, peace be upon them both, struck the earth with his heel, and a spring of sweet water appeared, and the dry riverbed flowed, the palm tree became green and bore fruit, and its fruit ripened. Then it was said to her:

(p-332)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 25:

﴿And shake﴾ move (حَرِّكِي, harriki) ﴿toward you﴾ toward yourself ﴿the trunk of the palm tree﴾. Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi) said: the bā' (in bi-jidh') is extra (zā'ida), meaning: shake the trunk of the palm tree. ﴿It will drop upon you﴾ with the assimilation of the first tā' into the second (tā'): Makki, Madani, Shami, Abu 'Amr, 'Ali and Abu Bakr. The original form is tatasaqqatu with both tā's pronounced. "Tasaqqat" with a fatha on the tā' and qāf, dropping the second tā' and lightening the sīn: Hamza. "Yassaqqat" with a fatha on the yā' and qāf, and the sīn doubled: Ya'qub, Sahl, Hammad and Nusayr. "Tusaqqit" (from the mufā'ala form) by Hafs. "Tuskit, yuskit, tasquṭ and yasquṭ," with the tā' referring to the palm tree and the yā' referring to the trunk: these make nine readings. ﴿Ripe dates﴾ is a tamyīz (specification) or a direct object, according to the reading. ﴿Fresh﴾ (janiyyan) meaning tender. They said: dates are for women after childbirth, a custom from that time. It was also said: nothing is better for a woman after childbirth than ripe dates, nor for a sick person than honey.

The commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 26:

﴿So eat﴾ from the ripe dates, ﴿and drink﴾ from the stream, ﴿and let your eye be consoled﴾ with the pleasing child. ʿAynan is a specifying accusative (tamyiz, an accusative that clarifies the meaning of a verb), meaning: be content in your soul with ʿIsa, and cast off from yourself what has grieved you. [p. 333] ﴿If﴾ (fa-immā): its origin is "in mā." The conditional "in" was joined to "mā" and assimilated into it (idgham, the merging of two consonants). ﴿You see any human being, then say: Indeed I have vowed a fast to the Most Merciful﴾. That is: if you see a human being who asks you about your condition, then say, "Indeed I have vowed to the Most Merciful a silence and a restraint from speech." They used to fast from speech just as they fast from eating and drinking. It was also said that it was an actual fast, and their fasting in it was silence, so its obligation was the obligation of silence. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) forbade the fast of silence, so that ruling was abrogated (naskh, the cancellation of an earlier ruling by a later one) for us. She was only commanded to vow silence because ʿIsa (peace be upon him) would suffice her by speaking in a way that would clear her innocence, and so that she would not argue with the foolish. In this is evidence that silence in the face of a fool is obligatory, and no fool has been restrained by anything like aversion, nor has his rein been loosened by anything like rebuke. She informed them that she had vowed the fast only by gesture, and a gesture may be called speech and utterance. Do you not see the poet's saying in describing graves:

"And they spoke concerning faces that will decay..."

It was also said that the obligation of silence came after this speech, or that this measure of speech was permitted to her. ﴿So I will not speak today to any human being﴾, meaning, to any mortal (insī, a human being).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 27:

﴿Then she brought him﴾ (i.e., Jesus) ﴿to her people﴾ after she had become pure from her postnatal bleeding (nifas), ﴿carrying him.﴾ This is a circumstantial clause (hal) from her; meaning, she came toward them carrying him. When they saw him with her, ﴿they said: "O Mary, you have certainly come with something monstrous (shay'an fariyyan)!"﴾ — that is, something novel and wondrous. And al-fary (the root meaning of fariyy) is "cutting," as if she were cutting off the usual course of things.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 28:

﴿O sister of Aaron﴾. He was her brother from her father, and he was among the most excellent of the Children of Israel. Or it means: he was the brother of Musa, peace be upon him, and she was among his descendants, and between them was a thousand years. This is like the saying "O brother of Hamadan," meaning: O one of them, or a righteous man or a wicked man in her time. They likened her to him in righteousness, or they reviled her by him. ﴿Your father was not a man of evil﴾, namely ʿImran, ﴿an adulterer﴾, ﴿and your mother was not an unchaste woman﴾, namely Hannah, ﴿an adulteress﴾. (p-334)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 29:

﴿So she pointed to him﴾ — to Jesus, that he should answer them. That is because Jesus, peace be upon him, said to her: "Do not grieve, and leave the answer to me." It was also said that Jibril commanded her to do so. When she pointed to him, they became angry and marvelled, and ﴿they said: "How can we speak to one who is﴾ [a child who] came into being and was found ﴿in the cradle﴾ (al-mahd), the well-known cradle, ﴿a child﴾ (sabiyyan) — a circumstantial accusative (hal)."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 30:

﴿He said: Indeed I am the servant of Allah﴾. When Allah had silenced her speaking tongue by His command, Allah made the silent tongue speak, so that he acknowledged servanthood (ʿubudiyya) while he was forty nights old, or one day old. It is narrated that he pointed with his index finger and said in a loud voice: "Indeed I am the servant of Allah." In this there is a refutation of the saying of the Christians: ﴿He has given me the Scripture﴾ (the Injil) ﴿and made me a prophet﴾. It is narrated from al-Hasan that he was a prophet in the cradle, and his speech was his miracle. It was also said that its meaning is: that this was decreed in His decree, or that what is to come was made certain, as if it had already occurred.

﴿And He has made me blessed wherever I may be﴾ — beneficial wherever I am, or a teacher of good (khayr). ﴿And He has enjoined upon me﴾ — and commanded me ﴿to observe the prayer and to give zakat﴾ — if I come to possess wealth. It is also said that it refers to zakat al-fitr, or to the purification of the body. It is also possible that the meaning is: "He has enjoined upon me that I command you to observe the prayer and to give zakat." ﴿As long as I live﴾ — accusative as an adverb of time (ẓarf), meaning: for the duration of my life.

ﷺ translation of the passage:

"And dutiful to my mother" (وَبَرًّا بِوالِدَتِي), conjoined with "blessed" (مُبارَكًا), meaning: dutiful to her, honouring her and magnifying her. "And He has not made me a tyrant" (وَلَمْ يَجْعَلْنِي جَبّارًا), arrogant (مُتَكَبِّرًا), "wretched" (شَقِيًّا), disobedient to parents (عاقًّا).

Note on the Qur'anic quotations: the verse is rendered as: "And dutiful to my mother; and He has not made me a tyrant, wretched."

﴿And peace is upon me the day I was born﴾. "Yawma" (the day) is an adverbial complement (ẓarf), and the element governing it is the predicate, which is "ʿalayya" (upon me). ﴿And the day I die and the day I am raised alive﴾. That is, that peace directed at Yahya in the three situations is directed at me, if the definite article (ḥarf al-taʿrīf) is for a specific reference (al-ʿahd). If it is for the category as a whole (al-jins), then the meaning is: and the category of peace is upon me. In this there is an allusion (taʿrīḍ) to a curse upon the enemies of Maryam and her son, because when he says "and the category of peace is upon me," he has implicitly indicated that its opposite is upon you, since the context is one of denial and obstinacy, so it was a sign (maʾinnah) of this kind of allusion. (p-335)

ذَلِكَ (Dhālika, "that") is the subject (mubtada'), ʿĪsā is its predicate (khabar), and Ibn Maryam is its attribute (naʿt), or a second predicate. That is: "that one who said, 'Indeed I am such-and-such'" is ʿĪsā son of Maryam, not as the Christians say, that he is God or the son of God. ﴿qawla l-ḥaqq﴾ (the word of truth) means the Word of God (kalimat Allāh). Here al-qawl means al-kalima (the word), and al-ḥaqq means Allah. He was called the Word of God because he came into being by His saying "Be" (kun), without an intermediary father. Its nominative case (irtifāʿ) is either because it is a predicate following a predicate, or the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtada' maḥdhūf), or an appositive (badal) of ʿĪsā. Its accusative case (naṣb) is read by al-Shāmī and ʿĀṣim, as an expression of praise (ʿalā l-madḥ) or as a verbal noun (ʿalā l-maṣdar), meaning: "I say the word of truth: he is the son of Maryam, and he is not a god, as they claim." ﴿alladhī fīhi yamtarūn﴾ (about which they doubt) means they hesitate, from al-miryah (doubt), i.e., al-shakk (uncertainty); or they dispute, from al-mirāʾ (disputation). So the Jews said, "He is a sorcerer, a liar," and the Christians said, "He is the son of God and the third of three."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 35:

﴿It is not for Allah﴾: it is not fitting for Him ﴿to take a son﴾. The particle min (from) is brought in to emphasise the negation. ﴿Glory be to Him!﴾: He declares Himself exalted above taking a son. ﴿When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾: the verb yakun is in the accusative (fa-yakuna) according to Ibn 'Amir (al-Shami), meaning: just as He said to 'Isa, "Be," and he was, without a father. Whoever is characterised by this is exalted above resembling a living being that begets offspring.

**Madarik al-Tanzil** (Commentary of al-Nasafi) on Surah 19, verse 36:

﴿Indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him.﴾ Read with a kasra on the *inna* (إنَّ) by al-Shami and al-Kufi, as a fresh sentence (*al-ibtida'*, meaning the beginning of a new sentence). It is part of the speech of Jesus, meaning: just as I am His servant, so you are His servants, and it is incumbent upon me and upon you to worship Him. Whoever reads it with a fatha (*anna*, أنَّ) treats it as conjoined (*'atf*) to "بِالصَلاةِ" (*bi-al-salah*, "with prayer"), meaning: "and He has enjoined upon me prayer and zakat, and that Allah is my Lord and your Lord." Or he makes it dependent (*ta'liq*) on what follows, meaning: "And because Allah is my Lord and your Lord, worship Him." ﴿This﴾, which I have mentioned, ﴿is a straight path﴾, so worship Him and do not associate anything with Him.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 37:

﴿Then the factions (al-ahzab) differed among themselves.﴾ Al-hizb (faction) is a group that stands apart from others in its opinion. There were three factions: the Nestorians (Nasturiyya), the Jacobites (Ya'qubiyya), and the Melkites (Malkaniyya). ﴿Among them﴾ means from among their own companions, or from among their own people, or from among mankind in general. This is because the Christians differed about Jesus when he was raised up, and then they agreed to refer to the saying of three men who were, among them, (p-336) the most learned people of their time: Ya'qub, Nastur and Malkan. Ya'qub said, "He is God, who descended to the earth and then ascended to the heaven." Nastur said, "He was the son of God, whom God manifested as He willed and then raised up to Himself." The third said, "They have lied. He was a created servant and a prophet." Each of them was followed by a people. ﴿So woe to those who disbelieved﴾ from among the factions, since each one of them was upon the truth ﴿from the scene of a tremendous day﴾. It is the Day of Resurrection, or it means from their witnessing the terror of the reckoning and the recompense on the Day of Resurrection, or from the testimony of that day against them, and that the angels, the prophets and their own limbs will bear witness against them to their disbelief, or it means from the place of testimony or its time. Or the intended meaning is the day of their gathering to deliberate about it. Its being described as "tremendous" is due to the monstrousness of what they bore witness to concerning Jesus.

The majority of scholars (al-Jumhur) hold that its wording is an imperative but its meaning is amazement (al-ta'ajjub). God, exalted be He, cannot be described as being amazed. Rather, what is intended is that their hearing and their seeing are worthy of being wondered at, after they had been deaf and blind in the world. Qatada said: "If they were blind and deaf to the truth in the world, then how much they will hear and how much they will see the guidance on the day it will no longer benefit them."

The word ﴿بِهِمْ﴾ ("with them") is in the nominative position as the agent (al-fa'iliyyah), as in the construction أكْرِمْ بِزَيْدٍ ("how generous is Zayd!"), whose meaning is: "Zayd is extremely generous."

﴿But the wrongdoers today﴾: the apparent noun has been placed in the position of the pronoun. That is, "but they today, in the world, by their wronging themselves, since they abandoned hearing and looking when it would have benefited them, and placed worship in other than its proper place." ﴿are in error﴾ from the truth, ﴿manifest﴾, clear. This refers to their belief that Jesus was a god to be worshipped, although the signs of contingency (al-hadath, i.e. createdness) were evident in him. This is a sign that there is no wrongdoing greater than their wrongdoing.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 39:

﴿And warn them﴾ of the day of their fear, ﴿of the Day of Regret﴾, which is the Day of Resurrection, because regret over what has been lost occurs in it. And in a hadith: "When they see their dwellings in Paradise, [they will say]: 'If only they had believed!'" ﴿When﴾ is either a substitute (badal) for "the Day of Regret," or an adverbial complement (zarf) of "regret," which is a verbal noun (masdar), ﴿when the matter has been decided﴾, meaning the reckoning has been concluded and the two groups have been separated, to Paradise and to the Fire. ﴿While they are heedless﴾, here, of giving attention to ﴿that station﴾ (p-337), ﴿and they do not believe﴾, meaning they do not affirm it. The two words "wahum" and "wahum" are both circumstantial clauses (hal), meaning: warn them while they are in this state, heedless and not believing.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 40:

﴿Indeed, We shall inherit the earth and whoever is upon it﴾. That is: We alone possess the dominion and permanence when destruction and annihilation have encompassed all. The mention of "man" (man) is to give precedence to those of intellect (al-'uqala').

﴿And to Us they will be returned﴾, with the yā' vowelled with a ḍamma and the jīm with a fatḥa (yuraj'ūna). Ya'qub (Ya'qub ibn Ishaq al-Hadrami) read the yā' with a fatḥa (yarji'ūna); that is: they will be sent back, and they will be recompensed with a fitting recompense.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 41:

﴿And mention﴾ to your people ﴿in the Book﴾ (the Qur'an) ﴿Ibrahim﴾, his story with his father. ﴿Indeed, he was a truthful (siddiq), a prophet﴾ without a hamza; Nafi' read it with a hamza. It has been said: al-sadiq (the truthful) is one who is upright in actions, and al-siddiq is one who is upright in states. Thus al-siddiq is of the intensive patterns (abniyat al-mubalagha), and its parallel is al-dhihhik (one who laughs much). The meaning is the extreme of his truthfulness and the great number of things he affirmed as true of Allah's unseen matters, His signs, His books and His messengers. That is, he was one who affirmed all the prophets and their books, and he was a prophet in himself. This clause came as a parenthetical insertion (i'tiradan) between Ibrahim and what is its substitute (badal) minhu, and it is

*When he said* It is permissible for *idh* ("when") to be connected either to *kān* ("he was") or to *ṣiddīqan nabiyyan* ("a truthful prophet"), meaning: he was combining the qualities of the truthful ones (*ṣiddīqīn*) and the prophets when he addressed his father with those addresses. The purpose of the Messenger's mention of him and his story in the Book is that he recite it to the people and convey it to them, like His saying: *"And recite to them the news of Abraham"* [al-Shu'ara': 69]. Otherwise, Allah, Mighty and Exalted, is the one who mentions him and presents him in His revelation. *"To his father, 'O my father'"* with a kasra on the *ta'*, but Ibn ʿĀmir read it with a fatha. The *ta'* is a substitute (*ʿiwaḍ*) for the possessive *yā'* (*yā' al-iḍāfa*), and one does not say *"yā abatī"* so that the substitute and what it replaces are not combined. *"Why do you worship what neither hears nor sees?"* The object in both is omitted, forgotten but not intended (*mansiyy ghayr manawiyy*). It is permissible to estimate it as: it hears nothing and sees nothing. *"And it does not avail you anything."* *Shay'an* ("anything") may be in the position of a verbal noun, meaning "anything of availing." It may also be a direct object, from your saying *aghni ʿannī wajhaka*, meaning: turn your face away from me, i.e., keep away. (p-338)

O my father, indeed there has come to me of knowledge ([what is meant is] the revelation, or knowledge of the Lord) that which has not come to you (﴿O my father, indeed there has come to me of knowledge that which has not come to you﴾). "Ma" in "ma la yasma'u" (that which does not hear) and in "ma lam ya'tika" (that which has not come to you) may be either a relative pronoun (mawsulah) or a descriptive noun (mawsufah). ﴿So follow me, I will guide you﴾ (ahdika): I will show you the way (urshidka) ﴿to a path that is even (sawiyyan)﴾, i.e., straight (mustaqiman).
﴿O my father, do not worship Satan.﴾ Do not obey him in what he embellished for you of worshipping the idol. ﴿Indeed, Satan has ever been disobedient to the Most Merciful.﴾ Disobedient.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 45:

﴿O my father, indeed I fear﴾ It was said: "[that it means] I know." ﴿that a punishment from the Most Merciful will touch you, so that you become a companion [walī] to Satan﴾, a companion in the Fire, who follows you and whom you follow. Consider his advice, how he observed courtesy (mujāmalah), gentleness (rifq) and good character, as he had been commanded. In a hadith: "It was revealed to Abraham: 'You are My intimate friend (khalīl). Make your character good, even with the disbelievers, and you will enter the entrances of the righteous.'" So he first asked his father for the cause of his error, the request of one who alerts him to his persistence and wakes him to his excess and extremity. For whoever worships the most noble of creation in rank, namely the prophets, would be deserving of manifest foolishness. How much more so is one who worships a stone or a tree, which does not hear the remembrance of its worshipper, does not see the forms of his worship, does not avert from him any affliction, and does not fulfil any need for him! Then he followed this with his call to the truth, being gentle with him and kind to him, so he did not label his father with extreme ignorance, nor describe himself with superior knowledge. Rather he said: "Indeed, there is with me some knowledge that is not with you," and that is the knowledge of guiding to the straight path. Suppose that I and you are on a journey, and I have knowledge of the way that you do not have; then follow me, and I will bring you out from going astray and wandering. Then he rounded it out (thalletha) by forbidding him from what he was upon, saying that Satan, who disobeyed the Most Merciful, from whom are all blessings, has led you into worshipping the idol and has made it attractive to you, so you are in reality its worshipper. Then he completed it (rabba'a) by frightening him of the evil consequence and what his present state drags him into of retribution (tab'ah) and calamity (wabāl). All of this observed proper manners, for he did not state explicitly that punishment would reach him or that torment would cling to him. Rather he said: ﴿I fear that a punishment will touch you﴾, using indefiniteness (tankīr), which indicates diminution, as if he said: "I fear that some small portion (nafayān, i.e., a little) of the punishment of the Most Merciful will befall you." He made Satan's guardianship and his entry into the company of Satan's followers and allies greater than the punishment, just as the good pleasure of Allah is greater than the reward itself. He began every piece of counsel with his words "O my father", seeking to win him over, to soften his heart, and to indicate the obligation of honouring the father even if he is a disbeliever. Then.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 46:

﴿Said﴾ Azar, in rebuke: ﴿Do you turn away from my gods, O Ibrahim?﴾ That is: do you turn away from worshipping them? He called him by his name and did not respond to "O my father" (yā abatī) with "O my son" (yā bunayya), and he placed the predicate before the subject, because it was more important to him. ﴿If you do not desist﴾ from reviling the idols, ﴿I will surely stone you﴾, that is, I will surely kill you by stoning, or I will surely strike you with stones until you go far away, or I will surely revile you. ﴿And leave me⁠﻿ alone﴾ is a conjunction with an omitted element indicated by "I will surely stone you"; its estimated form is: "so beware of me and leave me alone." ﴿For a long time﴾ is an adverb of time, that is: a long period of time, from al-milawa (the duration of a long time).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 47:

﴿Qāla salāmun ʿalayka﴾ — a salām of farewell and disengagement, or of closeness and gentleness. For this reason he promised forgiveness in his words ﴿Sa-astaghfiru laka rabbī﴾ — "I will ask my Lord to forgive you," i.e., I will ask Allah to make you among the people of forgiveness, by guiding you to Islam. ﴿Innahu kāna bī ḥafiyyā﴾ — gentle toward me through the generality of blessings, or merciful, or honouring; and ḥafāwah (tenderness) means compassion, mercy, and honour.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 48:

﴿And I will withdraw from you﴾. By withdrawal (i'tizal) he meant migration (muhajara) from the land of Babylon to al-Sham. ﴿And what you invoke besides Allah﴾, that is: what you worship of your idols. ﴿And I will call upon my Lord﴾, that is, I will worship my Lord. Then he said, out of humility and self-abasement, and as an indirect reference to their wretchedness in invoking their gods: ﴿Perhaps I will not be, in calling upon my Lord, unblessed﴾, that is: just as you have been wretched by worshipping idols.

(p-340)

When he withdrew from them and from what they worshipped besides Allah, ﴿and We granted him Isaac﴾, as a son, ﴿and Jacob﴾ as a grandson, a supplementary gift (nafilah), so that he might find comfort in them both. ﴿And each of them We made a prophet﴾. That is: when he left the disbelievers and the wicked for His sake, Allah compensated him with believing children who were prophets.

Translation:

﴿And We bestowed upon them of Our mercy﴾ meaning wealth and children. ﴿And We made for them a tongue of truth﴾ a good commendation, and it is the blessing upon Ibrahim and the family of Ibrahim in the prayers. He expressed by "tongue" what is found through the tongue, just as He expressed by "hand" what is applied by the hand, and that is a gift. ﴿Exalted﴾ elevated and renowned.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 51:

﴿And mention in the Book Moses; indeed he was chosen (mukhlaṣan)﴾. The Kufan reciters, other than al-Mufaḍḍal, read it with a fatḥah on the lam, meaning: Allah made him sincere (akhlaṣahu Allāh) and chose him (iṣṭafāhu). The others read it with a kasrah (mukhliṣan), meaning that he himself made his worship sincere for Allah, Exalted is He. So he is "mukhlaṣ" (one whom Allah has made pure) by the happiness he possesses through the original disposition (fiṭrah), and "mukhliṣ" (one who is sincere) in the worship incumbent upon him, through sincerity of resolve. ﴿And he was a messenger, a prophet﴾. The messenger (rasūl) is the one who has with him a book from the prophets; the prophet (nabī) is the one who gives news from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, even if he has no book with him, like Yūshaʿ (Joshua).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 52:

﴿And We called him﴾ — We summoned him and spoke to him on the night of Friday (laylat al-Jumu'ah) ﴿from the right side of the Mount﴾ — it is a mountain between Egypt and Madyan ﴿al-Ayman﴾ — from the right (al-yamin), i.e., from the direction of the right. The majority (al-Jumhur) hold that what is meant is the right side of Musa, peace be upon him, because a mountain has no right side. The meaning is that when he came from Madyan heading for Egypt, he was called from the tree, and it was at the side of the mountain on the right of Musa, peace be upon him. ﴿And We brought him near﴾ — a bringing near of rank and station, not of place and location ﴿as a confidant﴾ — a state (hal), i.e., conversing in secret (munajiyan), like a nadim (boon companion) in the sense of munadim (one who converses in intimacy).

﴿And We bestowed upon him of Our mercy﴾, meaning: out of Our mercy and Our tenderness toward him. ﴿his brother﴾ is the direct object (مَفْعُول, mafʿūl). ﴿Hārūn﴾ is an apposition (بَدَل, badal, a substitute noun) for it. ﴿as a prophet﴾ is a circumstantial qualifier (حَال, ḥāl, circumstantial accusative), meaning: We bestowed upon him the prophethood of his brother. Otherwise, Hārūn was older than him in age. (p-٣٤١)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 54:

﴿And mention in the Book Isma'il﴾ — he is the son of Ibrahim, according to the most sound opinion. ﴿Indeed, he was true to his promise﴾, fulfilling it. He promised a man that he would remain in his place until the man returned to him, and he waited a year in his place until the man came back. And it is enough [to show his merit] that he promised himself patience in the face of slaughter, and he fulfilled it. It is also said: he never made a promise to his Lord except that he fulfilled it. He specified him with truthfulness of promise, although it exists in other prophets as well, as an honour for him, and because it was the most well-known of his characteristics. ﴿And he was a messenger﴾ to the tribe of Jurhum, ﴿a prophet﴾, informing and warning.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 55:

﴿And he used to enjoin on his family﴾ his ummah (community), because the Prophet is the father of his ummah, and his household (ahl bayt) is also his ummah. And in this is evidence that he did not compromise (lam yudahin) with anyone else. ﴿with the prayer and the zakat﴾. It is possible that these two acts of worship were singled out because they are the two mothers (umma) of the physical acts of worship and the financial acts of worship. ﴿And he was with his Lord well-pleasing﴾ It was read as "marḍuwwan" (mardūwan) according to the original form (ʿalā al-aṣl).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 56:

﴿And mention in the Book Idris.﴾ He is Akhnukh (Enoch), the first messenger after Adam, peace be upon him, and the first to write with the pen, the first to sew garments, the first to study astronomy (ʿilm al-nujum) and calculation (al-hisab), and the first to make scales (al-mawazin), measures (al-makayil) and weapons, and he fought the sons of Qabil (Cain). As for their saying that he was named "Idris" for his frequent study (dirasa) of the Books of God, it is not sound, because if it were on the form "Idhʿil" derived from al-dars, it would have only one cause of diptotism, which is being a proper name, and it would be declinable; therefore its being prevented from declension (al-sarf) is evidence of its being non-Arabic (ʿujma). ﴿Indeed he was a man of truth (siddiq), a prophet﴾. God sent down to him thirty scrolls (suhuf).

﴿And We raised him to a lofty place﴾. It is the nobility of prophethood and nearness to God. It was also said that its meaning is: the angels raised him to the fourth heaven, and the Prophet (ﷺ) saw him there on the night of the Mi'raj (the Night Journey and Ascension). From al-Hasan: to Paradise, for there is nothing higher than Paradise. That was because, on account of the abundance of his worship, he was beloved to the angels, so he said to the Angel of Death, "Let me taste death, so that it will be easy for me," and he did so by God's permission, and he came back to life. He said, "Admit me into the Fire, so that I may increase in dread," and he did so. Then he said, "Admit me into Paradise, so that I may increase in desire." Then he said to him, "Come out," and he said, "I have tasted death and come to the Fire, so I will not come out of Paradise." Then God, Mighty and Majestic, said, "By My permission he did it, and by My permission he entered, so leave him." (p-٣٤٢)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 58:

﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to those mentioned in the surah, from Zakariyya to Idris, ﴿upon whom Allah bestowed favour among the prophets﴾. The word "min" (from) here is explanatory (li-l-bayan), because all the prophets are recipients of Allah's favour. ﴿Of the descendants of Adam﴾: the word "min" here is partitive (li-l-tab'id). Idris was of the descendants of Adam, due to his closeness to him, since he was the grandfather of Abu Nuh (Noah). ﴿And of those whom We carried with Nuh﴾: Ibrahim was of the descendants of those who were carried with Nuh, since he was the son of Sam ibn Nuh. ﴿And of the descendants of Ibrahim﴾: and Isma'il, Ishaq and Ya'qub, ﴿and Isra'il﴾, meaning: and of the descendants of Isra'il, that is Ya'qub. They are Musa, Harun, Zakariyya, Yahya and Isa, because Maryam was of his descendants. ﴿And of those⁠﴾ may be taken as conjoined to the first and second "min" (of). ﴿Whom We guided﴾ to the excellent qualities of Islam, ﴿and chose﴾ from among mankind, or for the explanation of the Shari'ah and the unveiling of the truth. ﴿When the verses of the Most Merciful were recited to them﴾, meaning: when the revealed books of Allah were recited to them. This is a resumptive statement (kalam mustanaf) if you take "alladhina" as the predicate of "ula'ika"; if you take it as a qualifier of it, then it is the predicate. Qutayba read "yutla" with a ya' because a separator intervenes, and the feminine here is not a true feminine. ﴿They fell down prostrating﴾: they fell upon their faces, prostrating out of longing. ﴿And weeping﴾: weeping out of awe. It is the plural of "baki," like "sujud" and "qu'ud" in the plural of "saajid" and "qaa'id." In a hadith: "Recite the Qur'an and weep; and if you do not weep, then feign weeping." And from Salih al-Murri: "I recited the Qur'an to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in a dream, and he said to me: 'O Salih, this is a recitation, but where is the weeping?'" And one says in the prostration of recitation: "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High," three times.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 59:

﴿Then there succeeded them﴾, meaning: after these preferred ones came ﴿a succession﴾, who were evil offspring. (With a fatha on the lam, khalf denotes a good posterity, al-'aqib al-khayr.) According to Ibn 'Abbas, they were the Jews. ﴿They neglected the prayer﴾, meaning they abandoned the obligatory prayer. ﴿And followed their desires﴾, meaning the pleasures of the souls. It is reported from 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him): "Whoever builds high, rides the showy, and wears the famous..." (p-343). It is reported from Qatadah (may Allah be pleased with him) that it refers to this Ummah. ﴿They will meet Ghayy﴾, meaning the recompense of error (ghayy). Among the Arabs, every evil is ghayy and every good is rushad. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud: it is a valley in Hell prepared for those who persist in adultery, drinking wine, consuming usury, disobeying their parents, and giving false witness.

"Except one who repents"—turns back from his disbelief—"and believes" in accordance with its conditions—"and does righteous deeds" after his faith—"those will enter the Garden," (the reading of) "yudkhulūna" with a damma on the yā' and a fatḥa on the khā' is that of Makkī, Baṣrī and Abū Bakr—"and they will not be wronged in the least." That is: they will not be diminished in the least from the reward of their deeds, nor will it be withheld from them; rather it will be multiplied for them. Or: they will not be wronged in the least from wrongdoing.

**Jannat** (Gardens) is a *badal* (substitute, in apposition) for *al-Jannah* (the Garden), because the Garden comprises the Gardens of Eden, since it is a *jins* (genus). Alternatively, it is in the *nasb* (accusative) by way of *madh* (praise).

**'Adn** (Eden) is *ma'rifa* (definite), because it is an *'alam* (proper noun) for the meaning of *'adn*, which is residence. Or it is an *'alam* for the land of Paradise, because it is a place of residence.

﴿Which the Most Merciful has promised to His servants﴾, that is, His servants who repent, believe, and do righteous deeds, as was mentioned earlier. He also attributed them to Himself, and this *idafa* (genitive construction) indicates *ikhtisas* (specialization), and these are the people of that specialization.

﴿In the unseen﴾, that is, He promised it while it is unseen by them and not present to them, or they are absent from it and do not witness it.

﴿Indeed He﴾: the pronoun is either *damir al-sha'n* (the pronoun of the matter) or the pronoun referring to ﴿the Most Merciful﴾.

﴿His promise has been﴾, that is, His promised thing, which is the Garden, ﴿certainly coming﴾, that is, they will come to it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 62:

﴿They shall not hear therein﴾ in the Garden ﴿any idle talk﴾, meaning obscenity, or lies, or speech of no benefit whatsoever, which is what is discarded from speech. In this there is an admonition concerning the obligation of avoiding idle talk and guarding against it, since God has declared His abode, in which there is no obligation (taklif), free of it. ﴿Except the word "Peace"﴾. That is: rather, they shall hear "Peace" from the angels, or from one another; or it means they shall not hear therein anything but a saying by which they are kept safe from fault-finding and blame. This is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati', an exception not of the same kind as what precedes it) according to the majority. And it has been said: (p-344) the meaning of "salam" is the supplication for safety. Since the people of the Abode of Peace are free from needing supplication for safety, its outward form would belong to idle talk and superfluous speech, were it not for the benefit of honour it contains. ﴿And they shall have their provision therein morning and evening﴾. That is: they shall be brought their provisions in measure with the two ends of the day as in this world, since there is no night or day there. Rather, they are always in light, and they know the measure of the day by the lifting of the veils and the measure of the night by their lowering. Provision in the morning and evening is the finest of living among the Arabs, so God described His Garden with this. It has also been said that He intended the continuance of provision, as you say, "I am with so-and-so morning and evening," meaning continuance.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 63:

﴿That is the Garden which We cause to inherit from among Our servants⁠—﴾ i.e., We make it the inheritance of their deeds, meaning its fruit and its outcome. It has also been said: they inherit the dwellings that were meant for the people of the Fire had they believed, because disbelief is a kind of death in judgment. ﴿Whoever was God-fearing﴾ (taqiyyan), i.e., refrained from shirk.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 64:

From Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O Jibril, what prevented you from visiting us more often than you visit us?" Then the following was revealed: ﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord. To Him belongs what is before us and what is behind us and what is between that. And your Lord is not forgetful.﴾

The word tanazzul (descending) has two meanings: the meaning of descending gradually and at a measured pace (ʿala mahal), and the meaning of descending in general (ʿala al-itlaq). The first is more fitting here, meaning: our descent at times, from one period to another, is only by the command of Allah. ﴿To Him belongs what is before us and what is behind us and what is between that. And your Lord was never forgetful.﴾ That is: to Him belongs what is in front of us and behind us of places, and what we are in. So we have no power to move from one place to another except by the command of Allah and His will. He is the Guardian, the All-Knowing of every movement and stillness, and of every state that occurs. Heedlessness and forgetfulness do not befall Him. So how could we move about in His dominion unless He permits us to do so?

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 65:

﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them﴾ is either a substitute (badal) for "your Lord," or the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), meaning: He is the Lord of the heavens and the earth. Then He said to His Messenger, since you have come to know that He is characterized by these attributes, ﴿so worship Him﴾, that is, persist in His worship. ﴿And be steadfast in His worship﴾, that is, be patient in enduring the envy of the envious for the sake of worshipping the One worshipped, and be patient with the hardships for the sake of worshipping the Creator, that is, so that you may be able to perform it. ﴿Do you know anyone with His name?﴾ — a equal (shabih) and a like (mathal); or, does anyone bear the name of Allah other than Him, because the name is specific to the One who is truly worshipped. That is: if it is established that there is no one worthy of worship to whom the servants may direct worship except Him alone, then there is no escape from worshipping Him and being steadfast in its hardships.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 66:

Ubayy ibn Khalaf (ʾUbayy ibn Khalaf) crumbled a bone and said: "Will we be resurrected after we have become like this?" So there was revealed: ﴿And man says, "When I have died, shall I really be brought forth alive?"﴾ The governing element (al-ʿāmil) of "idhā mā" is indicated by the context, and it is "ubʿath" (I will be resurrected), meaning: "When I have died, I will be resurrected." Its being put in the accusative by "ukhraj" (I will be brought forth) is impossible, because what follows the lam of initiation (lam al-ibtidāʾ) does not govern what precedes it; so you do not say "al-yawma la-Zaydun qāʾimun" (today Zayd is indeed standing). The lam of initiation, when it enters upon the present-tense verb, gives the meaning of the present (ḥāl) and emphasizes the content of the sentence; but when it is combined with the particle of the future (ḥarf al-istiqbāl), it becomes purely for emphasis and the meaning of the present disappears. The "mā" in "idhā mā" is also for emphasis. So it is as if he said: "Is it really true that we will be brought forth from the graves alive, at the time when death and destruction have taken hold of us?" This is in the manner of denial and disbelief. The fronting of the adverbial phrase (al-ẓarf) and its placement after the particle of denial is because what follows death is the time when life is denied, and from this their denial arose.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 67:

﴿Does not man remember﴾ — Khafif (the lighter reading) is the reading of Ibn 'Amir (al-Shami), Nafi' and 'Asim, from dhikr (remembrance). The rest read it with a doubled dhal and kaf, and its original form is yatadhakkaru, as in the reading of Ubayy, with the ta' assimilated into the dhal, meaning: "Does he not reflect?" The waw is a conjunction that links "does not remember" to "says," and the interrogative hamza of denial has been placed between the conjoined element and the conjunction; the meaning is: "Does he say that and not remember the first creation, so that he would not deny the second creation? For that is more indicative of the power of the Creator, since He brought substances and accidents from non-existence into existence. As for the second, there is nothing in it but the assembling of existing parts and their return to what they were, gathered together after dispersal." ﴿That We created him before﴾ — before the state in which he now is, which is the state of his existence. ﴿and he was nothing﴾ — this is evidence for what we have explained, and for the view that the non-existent is not a thing, contrary to the Mu'tazilah.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 68:**

﴿So by your Lord, We will surely gather them﴾, i.e., the disbelievers who deny the Resurrection, ﴿and the devils﴾. The conjunction *wa* (و) is for coordination, and it carries the sense of *ma'a* (مع, "together with"), with greater precision: they will be gathered together with their companions from the devils who led them astray. Each disbeliever will be coupled with a devil in a chain. In God's swearing by His name, when it is attributed to His Messenger, there is an exaltation of the status of His Messenger.

﴿Then We will surely bring them forth around Hell, on their knees﴾. *Jithiyyan* (جثيًّا) is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), the plural of *jāthin* (جاثٍ), meaning crouching upon the knees. Its form is *fa'ūl*, because its original root is *juthuww*, like *sujūd* and *sājid*. That is, they will be dragged from the place of gathering (al-maḥshar) to the shore of Hell, dragged in the state in which they were at the place of standing, kneeling upon their knees, not walking upon their feet.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 69:

﴿Then We will surely drag out from every group (shi'ah)﴾ a party (ta'ifah) that followed (shā'at), i.e., followed a deviator (ghāwiyan) among the deviants (ghuwāt), ﴿of them, whichever is most insolent against the Most Merciful (ar-Rahman) in rebellion (ʿitiyyan)﴾ in audacity (jur'ah) or wickedness (fujūran). That is: We will surely bring forth from every party of the parties of error whoever is most rebellious, then the next most rebellious, and when they are gathered together We will cast them into the Fire in order of precedence, bringing forward the most deserving of punishment first, and then the next. It was also said that what is meant by "those most insolent, in rebellion" are the leaders, because their crime is doubled, since they are both misguided and misguiding.

Sibawayh said: ʾayyuhum (أيُّهم) is built on damm (ḍamm, the vowel of case-ending being fixed) because the first part of the clause that is its relative clause (ṣilah) has been dropped, which is "huwa" (هو) from "ashaddu" (أشَدُّ), such that if it were brought in, it would be declined in the accusative (naṣb). It was also said: "ayyuhum huwa ashaddu" (أيَهُمُّ هو أشَدُّ), and this is because the relative clause clarifies and specifies the relative pronoun (al-mawṣūl), just as the genitive complement (muḍāf ilayh) clarifies and specifies the annexed noun (muḍāf). So just as the deletion of the muḍāf ilayh in "min qablu" (مِن قَبْلُ) necessitates the building (binā') of the muḍāf, the deletion of the relative clause or any part of it must necessitate building. Its position is accusative (naṣb) by "nanziʿu" (نَنْزِعُ).

Al-Khalil said: it is declined (muʿrabah), and it is a subject (mubtada') with "ashaddu" as its predicate (khabar), and it is nominative (raf') by way of hikayah (quotation). Its estimate is: "We will surely drag out those of whom it is said ʾayyuhum ashaddu ʿalā al-Raḥmāni ʿitiyyan (أيُّهم أشَدُّ عَلى الرَحْمَنِ عِتِيًّا)."

It is also permissible that the dragging out falls upon "from every party," like His saying ﴿And We bestowed upon them of Our mercy﴾ [Maryam: 50], meaning: We will surely drag out some of every party. So it is as if someone said: "Who are they?" and it was answered: (p-347) "ayyuhum ashaddu ʿitiyyan." And ʿalā (عَلى) is connected to "afʿal" (أفْعَلُ), meaning: their rebellion is most severe against the Most Merciful.

Translation:

﴿Then We are most knowing of those who are most deserving of it﴾, most worthy of the Fire, ﴿to be burned therein﴾. The word ﴿صِلِيًّا﴾ (ṣiliyyan) is a tamyiz (specification of the noun, i.e., a grammatical accusative clarifying the sense), meaning: entering (into it). The bāʼ (“in/with”) in ﴿بِها﴾ is connected to ﴿أوْلى﴾ (awlā, “more deserving”).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 71:

﴿And there is not one of you﴾ except that he will ﴿arrive at it﴾, i.e., enter it. What is meant is the Fire, and al-wurud (arrival) means entering. This is the view of ʿAli and Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and it is the view of the majority of Ahl al-Sunnah, based on His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So He will lead them into the Fire﴾ [Hud: 98], and His saying, ﴿If these had been gods, they would not have entered it﴾ [al-Anbiya: 99], and His saying, ﴿Then We will save those who had taremained conscious of Allah﴾ [Maryam: 72], since salvation only occurs after entering. And based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Al-wurud is entering. No righteous or wicked person will remain who does not enter it. It will be cool and safe for the believers, just as it was for Ibrahim." And the Fire will say to the believers: "Pass over, O believer, for your light has extinguished my flame."

It has also been said that al-wurud means entering, but that it is specific to the disbelievers, based on the reading of Ibn ʿAbbas, "wa-in minhum" (and there is not one of them). The well-known reading is then understood as a shift in address (iltifat).

It is related from ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud) that al-wurud means presence (hudur), based on His saying, ﴿And when he arrived at the water of Madyan﴾ [al-Qasas: 23], and His saying, ﴿Those will be kept far from it﴾ [al-Anbiya: 101]. This was answered by saying that what is meant is that they will be kept far from its punishment.

It is related from al-Hasan and Qatadah that al-wurud is passing over the Sirat, because the Sirat is stretched over the Fire; the people of Paradise will be safe, while the people of the Fire will be flung about.

It is related from Mujahid that the believer's arrival at the Fire is the touch of fever upon his body in this world, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Fever is the portion of every believer from the Fire."

A man from among the Companions said to another: "Are you certain of the arrival?" He said: "Yes." He said: "And are you certain of the return?" He said: "No." He said: "Then why laughter? And why heaviness?"

﴿It was a decree of your Lord, a matter decided﴾, i.e., their arrival was a necessary thing, decreed and determined (kaʾinan mahtuman). Al-hatm is the verbal noun of hatama al-amr, when he made the matter obligatory, and so the thing made obligatory is named by it, as in their saying "daraba al-amir" (the ruler decreed a beating).

Then We shall deliver those who were god-fearing (ʿAlī reads it with the lighter pronunciation, nunajjī) ﴿Then We shall deliver﴾ [the reading of ʿAlī uses the lightened form] ﴿those who feared God﴾ from polytheism, and they are the believers, ﴿and We shall leave the wrongdoers therein on their knees﴾. In this there is evidence that all [of them] enter [the Fire], because He said "wa-nadharu" ("and We shall leave") and did not say "wa-nudkhiluhu" ("and We shall cause them to enter"). The position [of the Sunnis] is that the person who commits a major sin may be punished in proportion to his sin, and then he will certainly be saved. The vile Murji'ah said he is not punished, because sin does not harm together with Islam according to them. The Mu'tazilah said he is eternally punished (yukhallad).

﴿When Our verses are recited to them as clear proofs﴾, that is, the Qur'an, ﴿clear﴾ in their evident inimitability (i'jaz), or as proofs and demonstrations. The phrase ﴿clear﴾ is a confirmatory circumstantial clause (hal mu'akkida), like His saying ﴿And it is the truth, confirming what is with them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 91], since the verses of God are never anything but manifest and conclusive proofs. ﴿Those who disbelieved said﴾, that is, the polytheists of Quraysh, who had combed their hair and dressed themselves ostentatiously, ﴿to those who believed﴾, meaning the poor, whose heads were disheveled and whose garments were coarse: ﴿Which of the two groups is better in position﴾, we or you, ﴿and better in assembly?﴾

On the word ﴿maqāman﴾: with a fatha on the mim, it denotes the place of standing, and what is meant is a place and a dwelling. With a damma (maqāman), Makki (one of the Qur'anic readers) read it, and it denotes the place of residence and abode. ﴿Nadiyyan﴾ means a gathering where people assemble for consultation (mashwara).

The meaning of the verse is that God, exalted is He, says: when We send down a verse containing evidences and proofs, they turn away from reflecting upon it and instead take pride in wealth, property, a fine dwelling and a good condition. Then God, exalted is He, said:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 74:

﴿And how many generations We destroyed before them⁠—﴾ "Kam" (how many) is the object of "ahlakna" (We destroyed), and "min" (from) is explanatory (tabyin), clarifying the vagueness of "kam"; that is, We destroyed many generations (qurun). Every people of an age is a qarn (generation) for those who come after them. ﴿Who were better in equipment⁠﴾ "Hum ahsanu" is in the accusative position as a description (sifah) of "kam". Do you not see that if you omitted them, "ahsanu" would be in the accusative as a description?

﴿Atha'than (equipment)⁠﴾ is the furniture of the house, or what is new of the rugs. ﴿Wa-ri'yan (and outward appearance)⁠﴾ means appearance and form. It is a verb in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ul), from "ra'aytu" (I saw). "Riyyan" without a hamzah and with a shaddah is read by Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir, by changing the hamzah into a ya' because it is sakin and what precedes it is kasrah, then by idgham (assimilation). Or it is from "al-riyy" (satiety, abundance), which is the blessing (ni'mah).

(p-349)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 75:

﴿Say: Whoever is in error (al-dalala), that is, in disbelief (al-kufr), let the Most Merciful extend for him an extension﴾ — the answer to "whoever" (man), since it is a conditional (shartiyya) clause, and this imperative is in the sense of a statement (khabar). That is: whoever disbelieves, the Most Merciful extends for him, meaning He gives him respite (amhalahu) and lets him live long (amla lahu fi al-ʿumr), so that he may increase in rebellion and error, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, We give them respite only that they may increase in sin﴾ [Al ʿImran: 178]. It was expressed in the form of a command to signify that this is obligatory and that it will certainly occur, like the one commanded who complies, in order that the excuses of the astray be cut off. ﴿Until, when they see what they are promised﴾ — this is connected to His saying ﴿better in station and finer in assembly﴾ [Maryam: 73], and what lies between them is a parenthetical insertion (iʿtiraḍ). That is: they will not cease saying this statement until they witness the promised thing with their own eyes. ﴿Either the punishment﴾ in this world, which is the Muslims' punishing them by killing and capture, ﴿or the Hour﴾, that is, the Resurrection, and what will befall them of disgrace and torment. So these two are substitutions (badal) for "what they are promised." ﴿Then they will know who is worse in place﴾ (manzilan) ﴿and weaker in forces﴾ (aʿwanan wa-anṣaran), that is: then they will know that the matter is the reverse of what they had estimated, and that they are worse in place and weaker in forces, not better in station and finer in assembly, and that the believers are the opposite of their description. It is also permissible for it to be connected to what immediately precedes it, and the meaning is: those who are in error are granted an extension in their error; they do not cease from their error until they witness God's support of the believers or see the Hour. And "until" (ḥattā) here is the one after which sentences are narrated; do you not see that the conditional clause follows it, namely His saying, ﴿when they see what they are promised, then they will know﴾ [al-Jinn: 24].

﴿وَيَزِيدُ اللهُ الَّذِينَ اهْتَدَوْا هُدًى﴾ "And Allah increases those who are guided in guidance." It is conjoined (ma'tuf) to the grammatical position (mawdi') of "فَلْيَمْدُدْ" (fal-yamdud, "let him extend"), because that phrase occupies the position of the predicate (khabar). Its implied sense is: whoever is in error, the Most Merciful extends (to him his respite), or "yamuddu lahu al-Rahmanu" (the Most Merciful extends it for him). "وَيَزِيدُ" means: He increases the misguidance of the misguided by forsaking them, and He increases "الْمُهْتَدِينَ" (al-muhtadin, those who are guided), that is, the believers, "هُدًى" (hudan, guidance) by way of steadfastness upon guidance, or by way of certainty and insight through His granting success.

﴿وَالْبَاقِيَاتُ الصَّالِحَاتُ﴾ "And the enduring good deeds": they are all the deeds of the Hereafter, or the five daily prayers, or "subhan Allah" (Glory be to Allah), "al-hamdu lillah" (Praise be to Allah), "la ilaha illa Allah" (there is no god but Allah), and "Allahu akbar" (Allah is greatest). ﴿خَيْرٌ عِنْدَ رَبِّكَ ثَوَابًا﴾ "are better in reward with your Lord" than what the disbelievers boast of. ﴿وَخَيْرٌ مَرَدًّا﴾ "and better in return," that is, better as a place of return and outcome. This is said in mockery (tahakkum) of the disbelievers, because they said to the believers (p-350) ﴿أَيُّ الْفَرِيقَيْنِ خَيْرٌ مَقَامًا وَأَحْسَنُ نَدِيًّا﴾ "Which of the two groups is better in station and finer in assembly?" [Maryam: 73]

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 77:

﴿Have you seen the one who disbelieved in Our signs and said, "I will surely be given wealth and children"?﴾ Thumma (here, ثَمَّ). With a ḍamma on the wāw and sukūn on the lām (وَلَد becoming وُلْد) in four places: here, in al-Zukhruf, and in Nuh, it is read by Ḥamzah and ʿAlī. It is the plural of walad (child), like ughsud for asad (lion), or it carries the meaning of walad, like al-ʿurb for al-ʿarab (the Arabs). Since seeing things is a path to knowing them and to the correctness of reports about them, they used "ara'ayta" (أرَأيْتَ, "have you seen?") with the meaning of "inform me" (أخْبِرْ). The fāʾ (فَ) conveys sequence (taʿqīb), as if he said: inform me also about the story of this disbeliever, and mention his account right after the account of those (earlier ones). And His saying ﴿I will surely be given﴾ (لأُوتَيَنَّ) is the answer to an implied oath (qasam muḍmar).

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 78:**

﴿Has he looked into the unseen?﴾ From their saying *iṭṭalaʿa al-jabal* (اطَّلَعَ الجَبَلَ), meaning he climbed to its top. The *hamza* (الهَمْزَةُ) is the interrogative particle, and the *hamzat al-waṣl* (همزة الوصل, the connecting hamza) is elided. That is, "Did he look into the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz) and see his end?"

﴿Or has he taken a covenant with the Most Merciful?﴾ That is, a binding pledge that He will give him that. Or *al-ʿahd* (العَهْدُ, covenant) means the word of testimony (*kalimat al-shahada*). It is reported from al-Hasan that it was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, but the well-known view is that it was revealed concerning al-ʿAs ibn Wa'il. It has been narrated that Khabbab ibn al-Arat (خَبّابَ بْنَ الأرَتِّ) made jewelry for al-ʿAs ibn Wa'il and then asked him for his wages. He said, "You claim that you will be resurrected and that in Paradise there is gold and silver. I will pay you there, for I will be given wealth and children then."

"Kalla" is a rebuke and a warning against error, meaning: he is mistaken in what he imagines for himself, so let him desist from it. ﴿Nay! We shall record what he says﴾, that is, his saying. The meaning is: We shall make it manifest to him and let him know that We have recorded his saying, because, as he said, it is written down without delay. God Most High said, ﴿He does not utter a word but that with him is a watcher, ready﴾ [Qaf: 18]. This is like his saying:

"When we claim lineage, a base woman did not bear me..."

That is: it becomes known and clear through the claim of lineage that I am not the son of a base woman. ﴿And We will extend for him of the punishment﴾: We will increase him in punishment, just as he increases in fabrication and audacity. It is from "al-madad" (extension); one says "madda-hu" and "amadda-hu" with the same meaning. ﴿Extending﴾ is emphasized with the verbal noun (madad) because of the intensity of God's Most High anger.

Qur'anic quotations: ﴿وَنَرِثُهُ ما يَقُولُ﴾ means "And We shall inherit from him what he says."

Here al-Nasafi explains: "That is, We shall take away from him what he claimed he would attain in the Hereafter. The meaning is: the referent of 'what he says' is wealth and children."

﴿وَيَأْتِينا فَرْدًا﴾ means "and he will come to Us alone." The word "alone" (fardan) is a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: without wealth and without children, as in His saying ﴿وَلَقَدْ جِئْتُمُونا فُرادى﴾ ("And you have certainly come to Us alone, as We created you the first time," Al-An'am 94). So his wishing and swearing (tamannihi wa ta'allihi) will avail him nothing.
