"And they have taken gods besides Allah" (﴿واتَّخَذُوا مِن دُونِ اللهِ آلِهَةً﴾), that is, these polytheists have taken idols which they worship, "that they may be for them a source of might" (﴿لِيَكُونُوا لَهم عِزًّا﴾), meaning: that they may take pride and strength through their gods, and that these gods may be for them intercessors and helpers who rescue them from the punishment.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 82:

﴿Nay﴾ is a rebuke to them for what they supposed. ﴿They will deny their worship﴾: the pronoun refers to the deities, meaning they will repudiate their worship and disavow it, saying, "By God, you did not worship us, and you are liars." Or it refers to the polytheists, meaning they will deny that they had worshipped them, like His saying ﴿By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 23]. ﴿And they will be to them﴾, that is, the things worshipped will be, for the polytheists, ﴿opposers﴾ (ḍiddan), meaning adversaries, because God, exalted is He, will give them speech, and they will say, "O Lord, punish those who worshipped us besides You." The word ḍidd (opposer) applies to the singular and the plural, and it stands in contrast to ﴿a source of might for them﴾ [Maryam: 81]. The intended sense is the opposite of might, which is abasement and humiliation, meaning they will be to them the opposite of what they intended, that is, they will be a source of abasement to them and not a source of might for them. If the pronoun in "they will deny" and "they will be" refers to the polytheists, then the meaning is: ﴿and they will be against them﴾, that is, their enemies, ﴿opposers﴾, meaning disbelievers in them after having worshipped them. Then He expressed astonishment to His Prophet ﷺ with His saying—

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 83:

﴿Have you not seen that We have sent the devils upon the disbelievers﴾ i.e., We let them be and them [the disbelievers], from: "arsaltu al-ba'ir" (I released the camel), I let it loose; or We gave them power over them through seduction. ﴿Inciting them to sin with incitement﴾: they urge them to sins with urging. The azz (ازّ) and the hazz (هزّ) are siblings [near-synonyms], and their meaning is: agitation and intense provocation.

﴿So do not be hasty against them﴾ with the punishment. ﴿We are only counting out for them a counting﴾. That is, We are only counting for them (p-352) their deeds for recompense and their breaths for their end. Ibn al-Sammak recited it in the presence of al-Ma'mun, and said: "If breaths are counted and have no replenishment, how quickly they will run out!"
﴿On the Day We will gather the God-fearing to the Most Merciful as a delegation﴾, riding on she-camels whose saddles are of gold, and on noble camels whose saddles are of rubies.

**Verse 86:** ﴿And We will drive the criminals﴾ — the disbelievers — ﴿like driving cattle﴾, because they were more astray than cattle, ﴿to Hell in thirst﴾ — thirsty — because one who comes to water comes to it only out of thirst. The real meaning of *wurud* (coming down to water) is going toward the water, and by it those who come are named *waridun*. Thus *al-wafd* is the plural of *wafid* (like *rakb* of *rakib*), and *al-warid* is the plural of *warid*. "The Day" (*yawma*) is governed by an implied verb: "the Day We gather," "and We drive," meaning: We will do to both groups what cannot be described; or, "Remember the Day We gather."

The mention of the God-fearing is that they will be gathered to their Lord, who has overwhelmed them with His mercy, as delegations come to kings to honor them; and the disbelievers are mentioned as being driven to the Fire as if they were thirsty cattle driven to water, in contempt for them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 87:

﴿They do not have the power of intercession﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). If the wāw (in yamlikūn) is taken as a pronoun, it refers to the servants, and its reference is indicated by the mention of the God-fearing (al-muttaqūn) and the sinners (al-mujrimūn), since they are divided into these two categories. It is also permissible that it be a sign of the plural, like the one in "akalūnī al-barāghīthu" (the fleas ate me), and the subject (fā'il) is "man ittakhadha" (whoever has taken), because it carries the meaning of the plural. The position (maḥall) of "man ittakhadha" is either nominative (raf') as a substitute (badal) for the wāw of "yamlikūn", or in the position of the subject (fā'iliyyah), or accusative (naṣb) by supposing an omitted genitive-modifier (muḍāf), meaning "except" the intercession (shafā'ah) of "man ittakhadha". The intended meaning is that they do not have the power that anyone should intercede on their behalf. ﴿Except for those who have taken a covenant with the Most Merciful﴾ by believing. In the hadith: "Whoever says, 'There is no god but Allah,' has a covenant with Allah." And it is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to his companions one day: "Would any of you be unable to take for himself a covenant with Allah every morning and evening?" They said: "And how is that?" He said: "He says every morning and evening: 'O Allah, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, I covenant with You that I bear witness that there is no god but You, alone, without partner, and that Muhammad is Your servant and Your messenger, and that if You leave me to myself, You bring me near to evil and distance me from good, and I trust only in Your mercy. So make for me a covenant that You will fulfil for me on the Day of Resurrection, for You do not break the promise.' When he says that, it is sealed with a seal and placed beneath the Throne. Then, when the Day of Resurrection comes, a caller calls out: 'Where are those who had a covenant with Allah?' and they enter Paradise." Or it may be from: "The commander (amīr) entrusted (ʿahida) so-and-so with such-and-such," when he ordered him to do it; meaning: none intercedes except the one who is commanded to intercede and is permitted to do so.
And they say, "The Most Merciful has taken a son" (Q. 19:88). That is, the Christians and the Jews, and whoever claimed that the angels are daughters of God.

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿Indeed you have brought something monstrous (iddan).﴾

He addressed them with this speech after having spoken of them in the third person, and this is an iltifat (shift of grammatical person); or He commanded His Prophet ﷺ to say this to them. Iddan (إدًّا): wonder, or something great and reprehensible. Iddah (إدَّةٌ): severity. Addani al-amr (أدَّنِي الأمرُ): the matter burdened me and weighed heavily upon me; adan (أدًّا).

﴿The heavens are nearly﴾ (تَقْرُبُ, *taqrubu*, "are close to") and with the letter yāʾ (ي): Nāfiʿ and ʿAlī. ﴿split apart﴾ and with the letter nūn (ن): Baṣrī (Abū ʿAmr), Shāmī (Ibn ʿĀmir), Ḥamzah, Khalaf and Abū Bakr. Al-infiṭār (splitting) comes from *fatarahu* (فَطَرَهُ), meaning "he split it" when he cracked it open, and al-tafaṭṭur comes from *faṭṭarahu* (فَطَّرَهُ), meaning "he split it" when he broke it into many pieces. ﴿from it﴾ means from the greatness of this utterance. ﴿And the earth is split open﴾ means it sinks in and its parts separate. ﴿And the mountains fall down﴾ means they collapse ﴿in ruin﴾, meaning broken into pieces or demolished. Al-haddah (the crashing sound) is the sound of a thunderbolt from the sky. The word *haddan* (هَدًّا) is a verbal noun, meaning "they crash down in a crash," from their saying (the utterance). Or it is an object of purpose (*mafʿūl lahu*), or a circumstantial state (ḥāl), meaning "crashing down" (*mahdūdatan*).

Surah 19, verse 91:

﴿That they ascribed a son to the Most Merciful.﴾ (p. 354)

Wait, let me translate the passage itself, as it stands:

"﴿An da'aw﴾, li-anna sammaw (because they named/ascribed), and its position (maḥall) is genitive by substitution (badal) from the ha' in "minhu," or accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), giving the reason for the collapse (al-khurur) by the crushing (al-had), and the crushing by the calling of a son for the Most Merciful; or nominative as the agent (fa'il) of "hadda," meaning: their calling crushed them, ﴿for the Most Merciful to have a son﴾" (p. 354)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 92:

﴿And it is not befitting for the Most Merciful (al-Rahman) that He should take a son.﴾ "Yanbaghi" is the reflexive form (muta'wi') of "baghā," meaning to seek. That is: it is not possible for Him to take a son, nor is it something that would be sought even if it were sought, since it is impossible and does not fall within the realm of what is valid. This is because taking a son is for need and for kinship of nature, and He is exalted above both of these. The specification of "al-Rahman" and its repetition several times shows that He alone is the Most Merciful, and no one other than Him deserves this name, because the roots and branches of all blessings come from Him. So let the covering be removed from your sight, for you and all that you possess are His gift. Whoever attributes a son to Him has made Him like one of His creatures, and by that has removed Him from deserving the name al-Rahman.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 93:

﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾. "Kull" (every) here is an indefinite noun described by a qualifying clause, "in the heavens and the earth," and the predicate of "kull" is "illa ati al-Rahman" (except that he comes to the Most Merciful). He made "ati" and "atihi" singular in agreement with the wording of "kull." It is an active participle from "ata" (to come), and it refers to the future, meaning: he will come to Him. "Abdan" (as a servant) is a circumstantial accusative (hal), meaning: submissive, humbled, and compliant. The meaning is: every one of those in the heavens and the earth, of the angels and of humankind, will come to God on the Day of Resurrection acknowledging servitude. Servitude and sonship are mutually exclusive, to the point that if a father owns his son, the son is freed upon him; and the relation of all of them to Him is the relation of the slave to the master. How, then, could some be a son and others a servant? Ibn Mas'ud read "ati al-Rahmana," in its original form before the addition (of the pronoun).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 94:

﴿Indeed, He has taken account of them and numbered them with an exact counting.﴾ That is: He has confined them by His knowledge and encompassed them.

"And every one of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection alone." That is, each one of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection in isolation, without wealth or children, or without any helper or supporter.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 96:

﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, the Most Merciful will appoint for them affection﴾ — affection (mawaddah) in the hearts of the servants. Al-Rabi' said: He loves them and makes them beloved to the people. And in a hadith: "The believer is given acceptance (miqah) in the hearts of the righteous and awe (mahabah) in the hearts of the wicked." And on the authority of Qatadah and Haram (p-355): "No servant draws near to Allah except that Allah draws the hearts of the servants toward him." And on the authority of Ka'b: "Praise does not settle for a servant on earth until it settles for him in the heavens."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 97:

﴿So indeed We have made it easy﴾ we made the Qur'an easy ﴿in your tongue﴾ in your language. (It is) a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) ﴿that you may give glad tidings thereby to the God-fearing﴾ the believers ﴿and warn thereby a people who are lud﴾ fierce in contentious dispute based on falsehood, i.e., those who take up every ladīd, that is, every intense (shaqq) kind of wrangling and disputation. It is the plural of alladd, and by it he means the people of Makkah.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 19, verse 98:

﴿And how many generations have We destroyed before them?﴾ This is a warning and a threat to them. ﴿Do you perceive any of them, or hear from them a whisper?﴾ That is: do you find, see, or know? The "ihsas" (perception) is the apprehension through a sense (ḥāssa). ﴿Or hear from them a whisper?﴾ A faint sound. From it comes the word "rikāz" (buried treasure, a hidden sound). That is: when Our punishment came upon them, no person remained who could be seen, nor any sound that could be heard. The meaning is that they were all destroyed. So likewise these people, if they turn away from reflecting on what has been revealed to you, their end will be destruction. So let their affair not trouble you. And God knows best.
